outcome: Still open for cubic graphs as of 11 October 2026. Since 26 January 2024 the cubic case has gained finite-order verification (Ducoffe and Dumitru, arXiv 2609.28594: no counterexample among all cubic graphs of order at most 48), a larger finite bound restricted to bipartite cubic graphs (Tranquilli, arXiv 2608.02675: none of order at most 58, hence at least 60 vertices; an unverified forum post claims order at most 62), structural results on minimal counterexamples (Carr, arXiv 2605.22844; Ducoffe and Dumitru), and an AI-assisted computational lower bound for general minimum-degree-3 graphs (Garcia, arXiv 2609.04686: none on at most 23 vertices, weaker than the cubic bound of 30 already attributed to Royle and Markstrom). No event establishes a cubic counterexample or a proof of the cubic statement.
problem_asks: The bullet asks one yes/no question about cubic graphs: does every cubic (3-regular) graph contain a cycle whose length is a power of two, 2^k with k ≥ 2 (so length 4, 8, 16, ...)? Parts: (a) the universal claim over all finite cubic graphs; (b) the existence of such a cycle in each one. The bullet asks for no bound, no count, and no structural description. The general conjecture for graphs of minimum degree at least 3 contains this bullet as a special case, but the bullet's own statement is the cubic restriction, so a result on minimum-degree-3 graphs in general would settle it while a result on any proper subclass would not. A cubic counterexample would be a finite cubic graph with no cycle of length 2^k for any k ≥ 2. The Wikipedia bullet itself gives no cubic counterexample; the question is open as posed.

events.what_happened: Computer-search results attributed to Markstrom (Extremal graphs for some problems on cycles in graphs, Congressus Numerantium 171, 2004, pp. 179-192) and to Royle and Markstrom: four cubic graphs on 24 vertices whose only power-of-two cycle length is 16 (one of them planar, the Markstroem graph); cubic graphs of order at most 29 verified; any counterexample has at least 16 or 17 vertices (Royle's search through 15 vertices, per Garcia); any cubic counterexample has at least 30 vertices. Primary paper NOT read: all of this is from secondary sources (Wikipedia, MathWorld, Garcia 2609.04686, Ducoffe-Dumitru).
events.delivers: Restricted computations only: no counterexample of order at most 15 or 16 (order 17 per Wikipedia); no cubic counterexample of order at most 29 (so at least 30 per Wikipedia's citation); four 24-vertex cubic graphs that avoid 4- and 8-cycles but contain a 16-cycle, so they are not counterexamples. Scope: the cubic bound is the cubic bullet's own quantity, but it is a finite-order check of a universal claim.
events.remains: The universal claim for all cubic graphs of order 30 and above.
events.directly_checkable: The 24-vertex cubic graphs are explicit (Markstroem graph available in Wolfram Language as GraphData["MarkstroemGraph"], per MathWorld); each can be checked by enumerating its cycle lengths.
events.doubts: The minimum order of a general counterexample is disputed between sources: Wikipedia says 17; Garcia 2609.04686 says the published bound is 16 (Royle's search through 15 vertices in Markstrom 2004) and that the figure 17 has no primary support. Primary paper not read, so neither figure is verified here.
events.direction: Cuts against no claim: the 24-vertex graphs are near-misses that keep a power-of-two cycle, and the order bounds only exclude small counterexamples.
events.object: Four cubic graphs on 24 vertices, one planar (Markstroem graph), each with no 4- or 8-cycle and whose only power-of-two cycle has length 16. Found by computer search and explicit; they are not counterexamples. Cited by MathWorld and Garcia; graph not independently checked here.

events.what_happened: Salehi Nowbandegani, Esfandiari, Shirdareh Haghighi and Bibak, 'On the Erdos-Gyarfas conjecture in claw-free graphs' (arXiv 1109.5398, v1 25 Sep 2011; v3 7 Feb 2013). Hobbs asked whether the conjecture holds for claw-free graphs; the paper gives results 'in particular for cubic claw-free graphs'. Per a search-tool summary (not verified in the abstract I opened), it shows a cubic claw-free counterexample would need at least 114 vertices. Wikipedia also credits Salehi Nowbandegani and Esfandiari (2011) with a computer-search bound of at least 30 vertices for a bipartite counterexample; not read in the primary source.
events.delivers: Restricted to claw-free graphs. For cubic claw-free graphs, a counterexample would have at least 114 vertices (search-tool summary only). Says nothing about cubic graphs with claws.
events.remains: Cubic graphs containing induced claws (the general cubic case); all claw-free non-cubic cases.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; restricted-class result.

events.what_happened: Christopher Carl Heckman and Roi Krakovski, 'Erdos-Gyarfas Conjecture for Cubic Planar Graphs', Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 20(2) (2013), Article P7, DOI 10.37236/3252; published 9 April 2013. Proves the conjecture for 3-connected cubic planar graphs; the proof is long, partly computer-based, and uses discharging. Abstract read; full text not read.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for the class of 3-connected cubic planar graphs (all orders). It is a restricted class of cubic graphs.
events.remains: Cubic graphs that are not planar, not 3-connected, or both; the cubic bipartite case; the general minimum-degree-3 case.

checked_by.who: Electronic Journal of Combinatorics (refereed journal; referees not named in the page read)

events.direction: Proves the conjecture for the stated class, i.e. the answer is yes there.

events.what_happened: Geoffrey Exoo, 'Three Graphs and the Erdos-Gyarfas Conjecture' (arXiv 1403.5636, v1 22 Mar 2014; the author's header says 24 Dec 2013, but the arXiv date is the first public one). Three cubic graphs derived from the Buckyball, the Petersen graph and the Tutte-Coxeter graph: the first is a partial answer to a question of Heckman and Krakovski about the planar version; the other two 'appear to be the smallest known cubic graphs with no 2^m-cycles for m ≤ 4 and for m ≤ 5'. Abstract read.
events.delivers: Constructions of cubic graphs with no 2^m cycle for small m (m ≤ 4: order 78 per Ripatti and Garcia; m ≤ 5: order 450 claimed). These are finite avoidance constructions, not counterexamples to the conjecture, since they do not exclude larger powers of two. Garcia 2609.04686 later reports the order-450 lemma false and repairs it. The planar graph is a partial answer to a planar question.
events.remains: The conjecture itself for all cubic graphs.
events.directly_checkable: The explicit cubic graphs; the 78-vertex graph is the one whose minimality Ripatti reports.
events.doubts: The order-450 construction for m ≤ 5 is reported by Garcia 2609.04686 to have a false lemma (the Tutte-Coxeter graph contains 8-cycles that break it); repaired there and stated as verified by that author.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (no counterexample constructed). Off-scope for the question as asked; a construction on the f(k) side.
events.object: Cubic graphs on the buckyball (truncated icosahedron) base for the planar partial answer, and graphs derived from the Petersen and Tutte-Coxeter graphs with no 2^m cycles for m ≤ 4 and m ≤ 5. Explicit constructions.

events.what_happened: Julien Bensmail, 'On q-power cycles in cubic graphs', Discussiones Mathematicae Graph Theory 37(1) (2017), pp. 211-220, DOI 10.7151/dmgt.1926 (DOAJ lists the issue as Feb 2017). For q ≥ 3, arbitrarily large cubic graphs with no q-power cycles; for q = 2, arbitrarily large cubic graphs whose 2-power cycles all have length 4 only, or 8 only. NOT opened: the publisher PDF returned a certificate error, the DOAJ and HAL pages returned 403 and an access-denial page; the content here is from a search-tool paraphrase of the abstract.
events.delivers: For q = 2: arbitrarily large cubic graphs in which every power-of-two cycle has length 4, or every one has length 8. These still contain 2-power cycles, so they are not counterexamples. For q ≥ 3: a different base, off-scope for this conjecture.
events.remains: The q = 2 conjecture itself for all cubic graphs.
events.doubts: Abstract not read from the primary page; statement is from a search-tool paraphrase.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (constructions still contain powers of two); restricted families.
events.object: Families of arbitrarily large cubic graphs in which all power-of-two cycles have one fixed length (4 or 8). Explicit families per the paraphrase; construction details not read.

events.what_happened: Ripatti, 'Faster approach for exhaustive search over graphs with certain properties', BAIKAL 2017 conference (abstract paper 138). Reports that the smallest cubic graphs with no cycles of length 4, 8 or 16 have 78 vertices, establishing Exoo's 78-vertex graph as minimal and listing five others of that order. NOT opened: the PDF was binary and unreadable; the content here is from a search-tool summary.
events.delivers: Concerns cubic graphs avoiding 4-, 8- and 16-cycles (an f(4) quantity). Not a counterexample route: such graphs can still have 32-cycles or others. Off-scope for the question as posed.
events.remains: The conjecture for all cubic graphs.

machine_checked.system: Exhaustive computer search with McKay-style isomorphism-free generation (per the abstract paraphrase)

events.doubts: Not read in primary; figure from paraphrase. Garcia 2609.04686 Prop. 6.1 reports a restricted search giving 78 on the same base only.
events.direction: Off-scope; bounds a related avoidance quantity.
events.object: The 78-vertex cubic graph (Exoo's) with no 4-, 8- or 16-cycles, shown to be minimal by exhaustive search.

events.what_happened: Hong Liu and Richard Montgomery, 'A solution to Erdos and Hajnal's odd cycle problem' (arXiv 2010.15802, v1 29 Oct 2020; v2 19 Sep 2022; JAMS 36 (2023)). Among other results, an average-degree condition forces a power-of-two cycle: there is an absolute constant such that every graph with average degree at least it contains a cycle of length 2^k. Erdos's 1984 question was in average-degree form. Abstract read; full text not read.
events.revisions: v1 29 Oct 2020; v2 19 Sep 2022 'accepted for publication'; published JAMS 36 (2023), pp. 1191-1234 (per search-tool summary).
events.delivers: For graphs of large average degree (hypothesis: average degree ≥ an absolute constant), a power-of-two cycle exists. Via minimum degree, this settles the general conjecture when the minimum degree exceeds that constant (as erdosproblems.com states). It does not reach minimum degree 3, and cubic graphs have average degree 3 so they are excluded.
events.remains: The minimum-degree-3 case, which includes every cubic graph; the cubic bullet.

checked_by.who: Journal of the American Mathematical Society (refereed)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication (v2 'Version accepted for publication'; published JAMS 36, 2023 per search-tool summary)

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; different hypothesis (average degree) from the bullet (cubic). Settles only large-minimum-degree cases.

events.what_happened: Yuping Gao and Songling Shan, 'Erdos-Gyarfas conjecture for P8-free graphs' (arXiv 2109.01277, submitted 3 Sep 2021; published in Graphs and Combinatorics 38 (2022), per search-tool summary). Every P8-free graph (no induced path on eight vertices) with minimum degree at least 3 contains a cycle of length 4 or 8. Abstract read.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for P8-free graphs with minimum degree at least 3 (a restricted class, with a stronger conclusion: a cycle of length 4 or 8).
events.remains: Graphs containing induced P8, including most cubic graphs; the general and cubic cases.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; restricted class.

events.what_happened: P. J. Couch, B. D. Daniel and W. Paul Wright, 'Classes of cubic graphs containing cycles of integer-power lengths', Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 79(1) (2021), pp. 100-105. Answers a special case of Caro's question: graphs of minimum degree 3 in which the centres of induced claws form an independent set contain a cycle of length a^k for some a ≥ 2 and k ≥ 2. Abstract read.
events.delivers: A weaker, different conclusion: a cycle whose length is a power of some base a ≥ 2, not necessarily 2, for a restricted class (independent claw-centres, min degree 3). Off-scope as an analogue of the base-2 question; it covers only a subclass of cubic graphs (cubic graphs with independent claw-centres, which are claw-free or have claws whose centres are independent).
events.remains: Base-2 power-of-two cycles for all cubic graphs.
events.direction: Consistent with Caro's generalised question on a restricted class; not a base-2 result.

events.what_happened: Zhiquan Hu and Changlong Shen, 'Erdos-Gyarfas Conjecture for P10-free Graphs' (arXiv 2308.05675, v1 10 Aug 2023; v2 12 Aug 2023). Every P10-free graph with minimum degree at least three contains a cycle of length 4 or 8. Abstract read.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for P10-free graphs with minimum degree at least 3 (restricted class, stronger conclusion: 4 or 8).
events.remains: Graphs containing induced P10, including most cubic graphs; general and cubic cases.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; restricted class.

events.what_happened: Shariefuddin Pirzada, Mushtaq Shah and Edy Tri Baskoro, 'On 2-power unicyclic cubic graphs', Electronic Journal of Graph Theory and Applications 10(1) (2022), DOI 10.5614/ejgta.2022.10.1.24. Exhibits an infinite family of cubic graphs each containing exactly one power-of-two cycle ('2-power unicyclic'). The abstract also says the only 2-power cycle 'cannot be removed, implying that there does not exist a counter example for Erdos-Gyarfas conjecture'. Abstract read.
events.delivers: Cubic graphs with exactly one power-of-two cycle: consistent with the conjecture (they are not counterexamples). The authors' inference that no counterexample exists is asserted in the abstract and not argued there as far as the abstract shows.
events.remains: Whether some cubic graph has no power-of-two cycle at all.

checked_by.who: Electronic Journal of Graph Theory and Applications (refereed journal)

events.directly_checkable: The graph family is explicit in the paper; the single power-of-two cycle per member can be checked by hand on small members.
events.doubts: The abstract's inference 'implying that there does not exist a counter example' does not follow from the family alone (a family with one 2-power cycle is not itself a proof that no counterexample exists); the abstract gives no argument for it. Full text not read.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (not counterexamples).
events.object: An infinite family of cubic graphs, each with exactly one cycle whose length is a power of two. Explicit construction per the abstract; not read in full.

events.what_happened: Anand Shripad Hegde, R. B. Sandeep and P. Shashank, 'Erdos-Gyarfas conjecture on graphs without long induced paths' (arXiv 2410.22842, v1 30 Oct 2024; v2 11 Feb 2025). Using a computer search, proves the conjecture for P13-free graphs with minimum degree at least 3. Abstract read; full text not read. Venue not established.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for P13-free graphs with minimum degree at least 3 (restricted class; computer-aided per the abstract). Not an AI system: 'computer search' only.
events.remains: Graphs with induced P13 (which include many cubic graphs), the general and cubic cases.

machine_checked.system: Computer search (method not detailed in the abstract)

events.doubts: Computer-aided restricted-class result; the computer search's verification details were not read.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; restricted class.

events.what_happened: Avery Carr, 'Cycles of Length 4 or 8 in Graphs with Diameter 2 and Minimum Degree at Least 3' (arXiv 2508.19302, v1 25 Aug 2025; v2 1 Sep 2025; v3 27 Jan 2026; v4 30 Jan 2026). Proves every graph of diameter 2 with minimum degree at least 3 contains a cycle of length 4 or 8. A 12-page note accepted for the Bulletin of the Institute of Combinatorics and its Applications (per the arXiv comments). Abstract read.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for graphs of diameter 2 with minimum degree at least 3 (restricted class, stronger conclusion 4 or 8). Diameter-2 cubic graphs are a small subclass.
events.remains: Graphs of diameter other than 2, including most cubic graphs.

checked_by.who: Bulletin of the Institute of Combinatorics and its Applications (journal named in the arXiv comments; no referee named)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the note for publication (per arXiv comment; publication not confirmed)

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; restricted class.

events.what_happened: Bogdan Georgiev, Javier Gomez-Serrano, Terence Tao and Adam Zsolt Wagner, 'Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale' (arXiv 2511.02864, v1 3 Nov 2025; v2 15 Dec 2025; v3 22 Dec 2025). The paper has a section on the Erdos-Gyarfas conjecture (section 6.31 in the paper; problem 51 in the authors' repository, which states the problem verbatim and points to section 6.31). Per search-tool snippets only (not verified against the section text, which I could not read), the authors tasked AlphaEvolve with producing a counterexample by optimising a score that is negative unless one is found, and report no counterexample for graphs up to 40 vertices. I could NOT read section 6.31: the HTML was truncated before it and the PDF exceeded the fetch size limit.
events.delivers: Per the unverified snippet: a negative computational search (no counterexample found up to 40 vertices), with no claimed positive result. Delivers no settlement, no bound, and no restricted case as far as I could establish. Whether the section reports anything more is unknown.
events.remains: Everything in the problem.

checked_by.who: Javier Gomez-Serrano and Terence Tao (named in the authors' repository README as having supervised, selected problems and reviewed the work)
checked_by.what_they_did: Supervised, selected problems and reviewed the work overall (repository README). Nothing specific to this problem's section was read.

events.doubts: The AlphaEvolve outcome for this conjecture is known to me only from unverified search-tool snippets; another summary attributes to the paper a section number 4.28 and a result about large minimum degree, which conflicts with the section numbering I found (6.31). Neither was verified from the section text.
events.direction: Negative computational outcome on the cubic-or-general question, per the unverified summary; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Avery Carr, 'Every Minimal Counterexample to the Erdos-Gyarfas Conjecture is Predominantly Cubic' (arXiv 2605.22844, v1 13 May 2026; sole version). A minimal counterexample (minimum order and size) has minimum degree at least 3 and no power-of-two cycle. Results: every vertex is adjacent to a vertex of degree exactly 3; at least 4/7 of the vertices have degree exactly 3; every regular minimal counterexample must be cubic (an observation credited to Markstrom). Abstract and full HTML read; acknowledgements thank Markstrom for structural observations.
events.delivers: Structural properties of any minimal counterexample, none of which asserts or refutes existence. For the cubic bullet: a regular minimal counterexample must be cubic, and at least 4/7 of the vertices of a minimal counterexample have degree 3. Restricted to minimal counterexamples; nothing on cubic graphs in general.
events.remains: Existence of a counterexample at all; whether any cubic graph is a counterexample.
events.direction: Structural: no direction on existence. Cites Markstrom's observation.

events.what_happened: A post on the erdosproblems.com forum for Problem 64 by the user jul059 (26 Jul 2026, 16:32) claiming that in any minimal counterexample strictly more than 2/3 of vertices have degree exactly 3, improving 4/7, with the attribution 'Found by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol High, not verified.' Read through the fetch tool's summary; the post's full text and any attached proof were not captured, and the page reports 'Proof claims (3)' of which I identified only this one.
events.delivers: Per the post (unverified): every minimal counterexample has more than 2/3 of its vertices of degree 3. This is a structural bound on minimal counterexamples only, not an existence result.
events.remains: Existence of a counterexample; the cubic bullet itself.
events.doubts: The poster says the result is 'not verified'. Ducoffe and Dumitru later posted the same bound (2/3) in 2609.28594; the HTML I read does not cite this forum post. Whether the posted argument is the same proof, or independent, is not established.
events.direction: Structural bound; no direction on existence.

systems.name: ChatGPT 5.6 Sol High
systems.what_it_did: Per the poster, found the claimed structural bound (more than 2/3 of vertices of a minimal counterexample have degree 3); the poster marks the result as not verified.
systems.basis_quote: Found by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol High, not verified.

events.what_happened: Julius Tranquilli, 'A 60-Vertex Lower Bound for Cubic Bipartite Counterexamples to the Erdos-Gyarfas Conjecture' (arXiv 2608.02675, v1 2 Aug 2026; sole version; Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21695513; GitHub repository floor-licker/erdos-gyarfas-cubic-bipartite, not opened). Main theorem: every simple cubic bipartite graph on at most 58 vertices contains a cycle of length 4, 8 or 16 (certified exhaustive search, two independent C16 oracles, zero completions). Hence any cubic bipartite counterexample has at least 60 vertices. Read from the arXiv HTML.
events.delivers: For cubic bipartite graphs only: no counterexample of order at most 58, so a bipartite cubic counterexample would have order at least 60. Off-scope as a proper subclass of the bullet's cubic graphs. The paper says it does not examine order 60, so 60 itself is not excluded.
events.remains: All non-bipartite cubic graphs, and all cubic bipartite graphs of order 60 and above; the bullet's cubic statement in full.

machine_checked.system: Certified exhaustive search by the author's own code (triangle-rooted restricted-growth search), with certificates; no proof assistant

events.directly_checkable: The enumeration and certificates are in the public artifact (GitHub and Zenodo; not opened here).
events.doubts: Single author, v1 only; the author discloses substantial AI assistance (listed under ai), and states that the retained code, logs and certificates, not AI assertions, form the evidence. No human reading found. A later forum post (31 Aug 2026) claims a cubic bipartite bound of 62 on the same question.
events.direction: Finite verification in a subclass; consistent with the conjecture; no cubic counterexample.

events.what_happened: A post on the erdosproblems.com forum for Problem 64 by the user sallerk (31 Aug 2026, 06:10): an exhaustive search finds no cubic bipartite counterexample on at most 62 vertices, giving a lower bound of 64 for that class. The post says it does not advance the general cubic case, whose search reached only order 34 by its account. Read through the fetch tool's summary; no code or proof link captured.
events.delivers: Per the post (unverified): for cubic bipartite graphs, no counterexample on at most 62 vertices. Restricted to the bipartite subclass; extends Tranquilli's 58 by an unverified computation. Says nothing about non-bipartite cubic graphs.
events.remains: Non-bipartite cubic graphs; cubic bipartite graphs of order 64 and above; the cubic statement in full.
events.doubts: Unverified forum claim; no code, certificate or write-up captured. The post does not appear to cite Tranquilli (not checked in the captured text).
events.direction: Finite verification in a subclass; consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Daniel Garcia, 'Small graphs without power-of-two cycles: a lower bound of 24, a correction to a construction of Exoo, and explicit bounds for f(k)' (arXiv 2609.04686, v1 4 Sep 2026; sole version). Main theorem (Theorem 2.1): every graph with minimum degree at least 3 on at most 23 vertices contains a cycle of length 4 or 8, checked level by level by a SAT encoding with DRAT proofs (CaDiCaL 2.1.3, drat-trim; 'All twenty proofs were accepted'). Consequence: any counterexample to the conjecture has at least 24 vertices (general minimum-degree-3 statement, which also covers cubic graphs). Also: repairs Exoo's order-450 construction for f(5) (Exoo's lemma is false because the Tutte-Coxeter graph has 8-cycles), gives f(4) ≤ 78 as optimal among gadget designs, and f(6) ≤ 32640. Title-block footnote: 'Computations were carried out with the assistance of an AI system (Claude); all results were independently re-verified as described in Section 8.' Read from arXiv HTML and abstract; some passages through the fetch tool's summary.
events.delivers: For minimum-degree-3 graphs (which include cubic graphs): none on at most 23 vertices, so any counterexample has at least 24 vertices. For cubic graphs this is weaker than the cubic bound of 30 already attributed to Royle and Markstrom, so it moves no cubic bound. Other results concern f(k), a related avoidance quantity, not counterexamples.
events.remains: Existence of a counterexample at any order; the cubic statement in full.

machine_checked.system: SAT (CaDiCaL 2.1.3) with DRAT proofs checked by drat-trim; cycle-length checks by DFS and by SAT

events.directly_checkable: The SAT encodings and proofs; the cycle-length routine validated against Petersen, Heawood and dodecahedron graphs (per the paper's Section 8 as summarised).
events.doubts: The abstract (as read through the fetch tool) says the smallest counterexample 'therefore has exactly 24 vertices', while the stated theorem only gives a lower bound of 24 and Markstrom's 24-vertex cubic graphs contain 16-cycles. Read as an existence claim this is unsupported; read as a lower bound it is consistent. Single author; the AI assistance's role in computations is not specified in the text.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (finite verification for minimum-degree-3 graphs on at most 23 vertices).

systems.name: Claude

events.what_happened: Guillaume Ducoffe and Bogdan Dumitru, 'Towards a more structured search for Erdos-Gyarfas counter-examples' (arXiv 2609.28594, v1 23 Sep 2026; sole version). Structural: any minimal counterexample has more than 2/3 of its vertices of degree 3 (improving Carr's 4/7); it is biconnected or a 1-clique-sum of two biconnected graphs. Computational: using these properties and a SAT-based exhaustive search, the conjecture is verified for all graphs of order at most 40, all bipartite graphs of order at most 66, and all cubic graphs of order at most 48. The search produces no resolution proof; the paper says a search must be rerun to verify it. Read from the arXiv abstract and HTML.
events.delivers: Finite verifications: no counterexample of order at most 40 (all graphs), at most 66 (bipartite), at most 48 (cubic). Derived by me: since cubic graphs have even order, any cubic counterexample has at least 50 vertices; any bipartite counterexample has order at least 67. Structural: the 2/3 degree-3 fraction for minimal counterexamples. Neither part settles an infinite family.
events.remains: Cubic graphs of order 50 and above, i.e. the infinite cubic statement; the general conjecture.

machine_checked.system: SAT-based exhaustive search (own code; no resolution proof produced)

events.doubts: The verifications rely on a search without proof certificates (paper says a rerun is needed). The 2/3 bound is the same statement as a forum post by jul059 (26 Jul 2026, attributed to a model; see jul059-forum-2026); the HTML I read does not cite that post, so the priority question is open and recorded in disputes.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: no counterexample at the stated orders; structural constraint on minimal counterexamples.

disputes.summary: The bound that more than 2/3 of the vertices of a minimal counterexample have degree 3 (improving Carr's 4/7) was posted on the erdosproblems.com forum on 26 Jul 2026 by jul059, credited to 'ChatGPT 5.6 Sol High' and marked not verified. Ducoffe and Dumitru posted the same bound on 23 Sep 2026 without citing the forum post (in the HTML read). Which is first, and whether they are the same argument, is not established.

Minimum order of a general counterexample: Wikipedia and secondary sources say 17; Garcia (arXiv 2609.04686) says the published bound is 16 (from Royle's search through 15 vertices reported in Markstrom 2004) and that the 17 has no primary source. Not resolved here, and the primary Markstrom and Royle sources were not read.

Cubic bipartite bound: Tranquilli (2 Aug 2026) proves no counterexample of order at most 58; the forum post by sallerk (31 Aug 2026) claims order at most 62, unverified. Both are for bipartite cubic graphs only.
Prize discrepancy (not progress): Wikipedia gives $100 for a proof and $50 for a counterexample; erdosproblems.com lists a $1000 prize for Problem 64.

summary: Across all sources I opened, the cubic statement remains open at 11 October 2026, and every source that discusses its status (erdosproblems.com Problem 64, MathWorld, Garcia, Ducoffe-Dumitru, Wikipedia) calls it open. Since 26 January 2024 the cubic case has received finite verifications and structure, none of which is a proof or a counterexample: Ducoffe and Dumitru (23 Sep 2026) verify no cubic counterexample of order at most 48, which by even order gives at least 50 (a derived figure, not theirs); Tranquilli (2 Aug 2026) rules out cubic bipartite counterexamples of order at most 58 (so at least 60); a forum post (31 Aug 2026) claims 62 for the bipartite class, unverified. Carr (May 2026) gives structure on minimal counterexamples (4/7 of vertices of degree 3; a regular minimal counterexample is cubic). Garcia (4 Sep 2026) proves that minimum-degree-3 graphs on at most 23 vertices contain a 4- or 8-cycle, so any counterexample has at least 24 vertices; for cubic graphs this is weaker than the 30 attributed to Royle and Markstrom, so it moves no cubic bound. Restricted-class results before and within the window (Heckman-Krakovski 2013 for 3-connected cubic planar graphs; Gao-Shan 2021 for P8-free; Hu-Shen 2023 for P10-free; Hegde et al. 2024 for P13-free; Carr 2025 for diameter 2; Couch-Daniel-Wright 2021 for a base-a variant on a claw-centre-independent class; Liu-Montgomery 2020 for large average degree) are recorded with their scope. Pre-window constructions (Bensmail 2017, Ripatti 2017, Exoo 2014, Pirzada et al. 2022) show near-misses with cycles of length 4, 8 or 16 and are not counterexamples. The question of AI involvement has several parts. Three events involve AI with named systems: Tranquilli (OpenAI ChatGPT, OpenAI Codex, and an unnamed Codex-based harness, with a disclosure that the assistance included developing computational and structural approaches, preliminary arguments and running computations); Garcia (footnote: computations 'with the assistance of an AI system (Claude)', role not specified); and the forum post jul059 (credited 'ChatGPT 5.6 Sol High' for the 2/3 bound, marked not verified). The forum post sallerk discloses 'AI assistance' with no system named, so no system is recorded for it. The AlphaEvolve experiment in arXiv 2511.02864 (section 6.31) involved AlphaEvolve in a search for a counterexample, with a negative outcome per unverified snippets; I could not read the section text (HTML truncated before it; PDF over size limit), so no authors' sentence was quotable and no system is listed in ai.systems. The Ducoffe-Dumitru computations and the Garcia SAT proofs are computer-assisted, not AI. Whether Tranquilli's and Garcia's AI roles were load-bearing (the computations would otherwise have had to be established another way) is not settled by the text: Tranquilli's disclosure names AI for developing computational approaches and running computations, which reads as load-bearing; Garcia's does not say what Claude did. A namesake, the Erdos-Gyarfas conjecture on monochromatic path covers, is a different problem and is not recorded as an event here; search results pointed to a July 2026 preprint (Chen and Chen) and to an earlier result by Pokrovskiy, Versteegen and Williams for large n. Neither was opened.
competing_reading: The finite verifications and the 24-vertex and 2/3-fraction results could be read as moving a quantity the bullet names: the order of a smallest cubic counterexample. Ducoffe-Dumitru's order-48 check plus even order gives at least 50 for cubic counterexamples, up from 30, so a reader could say the cubic question has moved. Against that: the bullet asks a universal yes/no question, and finitely many verified instances of a universal claim move nothing under the scope rule; the bound on counterexample order is not a quantity the bullet asks for. On AI: Tranquilli's disclosure can be read as load-bearing (ChatGPT developed computational and structural approaches and ran computations; the paper says the code and certificates are the evidence) or as work around the mathematics (literature audit, drafting, code auditing by Codex). Garcia's footnote is compatible with a purely clerical role for Claude, since the text says nothing about what it did. The jul059 post could be read as an AI-credited discovery of the 2/3 bound (in which case AI is load-bearing for that event), or as an unverified forum note whose argument may not match the later proof; the record cannot tell which.
what_would_settle_it: For the cubic statement: a proof, or an explicit cubic graph with no cycle of length 2^k (k ≥ 2), with an independent checker. For scope: the full text of section 6.31 of arXiv 2511.02864 (score function, graph sizes, outcome, any model named) and the complete jul059 and sallerk forum posts with any attachments. For AI load-bearing: the Tranquilli GitHub artifact and activity log (the paper says the 'fuller activity-level account' is in the repository) and the Garcia Section 8 and author statement of what Claude did. For priority: the time-stamped history of the jul059 proof and whether it matches the Ducoffe-Dumitru argument.

judgement.why: The statement is a universal yes/no claim about all cubic graphs, so finite-order searches (Markstrom, AlphaEvolve, Tranquilli, sallerk, Garcia, Ducoffe-Dumitru) are instances, and the smallest-counterexample order is not a quantity the statement asks for. Structural facts about minimal counterexamples (Carr 2026, jul059, Ducoffe-Dumitru's 2/3 part) settle no class of cubic graphs: none. Proofs for infinite subclasses that contain cubic graphs (3-connected planar cubic; P8/P10/P13-free min-degree-3; diameter 2 min-degree-3) are cases. Liu-Montgomery (large average degree, excludes cubic), Couch et al. (base-a analogue) and the f(k) avoidance constructions (Exoo, Bensmail, Ripatti) are variants. Carr 2025 is digested on the strength of journal acceptance stated on arXiv. AI: Tranquilli's disclosure credits ChatGPT with developing approaches, code and preliminary arguments that feed the result — assisted; Codex and the harness did auditing, verification and drafting, so not credited. Garcia's footnote says only that computations were assisted, too thin to show mathematics from Claude: none. jul059 credits the model with finding the bound: generated, though the event scopes none. AlphaEvolve has no quote in systems: none.
judgement.doubts: AlphaEvolve section 6.31 unread; Carr 2025 acceptance known only from the arXiv comment; Salehi claw-free result could alternatively be read as a case if it proves something for all cubic claw-free graphs rather than an order bound — record cannot tell.
